functions.name: bibliography
functions.signature:
.bibliography path:{String} \
             style:{String = DEFAULT_CSL_STYLE} \
             title:{InlineMarkdownContent? = null} \
         breakpage:{Boolean = true} \
      headingdepth:{Int = 1} \
     numberheading:{Boolean = false} \
      indexheading:{Boolean = false}
-> Node

params.name: path
params.desc: path to the bibliography file, with extension

params.name: style
params.desc: CSL (https://citationstyles.org) style identifier (e.g. `apa`, `ieee`, `chicago-author-date`). See https://github.com/quarkdown-labs/kotlin-bibliographer/tree/main/styles for the available styles.

params.name: title
params.desc: title of the bibliography. If unset, the default localized title is used

params.name: breakpage
params.desc: whether the heading preceding the bibliography triggers an automatic page break. Enabled by default.

params.name: headingdepth
params.desc: depth of the heading preceding the bibliography

params.name: numberheading
params.desc: whether the heading preceding the bibliography should be numbered and have its position tracked in the document hierarchy. Implicitly enabled when [indexheading](bibliography.html) is enabled.

params.name: indexheading
params.desc: whether the heading preceding the bibliography should itself be indexed in the document's table of contents.

functions.doc:
```block lang-kotlin
.bibliography path:{String} \
             style:{String = DEFAULT_CSL_STYLE} \
             title:{InlineMarkdownContent? = null} \
         breakpage:{Boolean = true} \
      headingdepth:{Int = 1} \
     numberheading:{Boolean = false} \
      indexheading:{Boolean = false}
-> Node
```

Generates a bibliography from a bibliography file.

Supported formats include [BibTeX](https://www.bibtex.org) (`.bib`), CSL JSON, YAML, EndNote, and RIS.

The bibliography is formatted using a [CSL](https://citationstyles.org) style definition, powered by [kotlin-bibliographer](https://github.com/quarkdown-labs/kotlin-bibliographer), which embeds a curated selection of citation styles from the [CSL Style Repository](https://github.com/citation-style-language/styles).

Example:  

```block lang-markdown
.bibliography {bibliography.bib} style:{apa}
```

#### Return

an AstGroup containing an optional heading and a BibliographyView

#### Parameters

* **path**

  path to the bibliography file, with extension
* **style**

  CSL (https://citationstyles.org) style identifier (e.g. `apa`, `ieee`, `chicago-author-date`). See https://github.com/quarkdown-labs/kotlin-bibliographer/tree/main/styles for the available styles.
* **title**

  title of the bibliography. If unset, the default localized title is used
* **breakpage**

  whether the heading preceding the bibliography triggers an automatic page break. Enabled by default.
* **headingdepth**

  depth of the heading preceding the bibliography
* **numberheading**

  whether the heading preceding the bibliography should be numbered and have its position tracked in the document hierarchy. Implicitly enabled when [indexheading](bibliography.html) is enabled.
* **indexheading**

  whether the heading preceding the bibliography should itself be indexed in the document's table of contents.

#### See also

* [cite](cite.html)

  to cite bibliography entries

#### Throws

* [java.io.IOException](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/io/IOException.html)

  if the bibliography file cannot be read or parsed
* [IllegalArgumentException](https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin/-illegal-argument-exception/index.html)

  if the specified style does not exist or is invalid

#### Permissions

* project-read to read bibliography files located in the project directory
* global-read to read bibliography files located outside the project directory

#### Wiki page

[bibliography](https://quarkdown.com/wiki/bibliography)

functions.name: cite

params.name: key
params.desc: the key (or comma-separated keys) of the bibliography entries to cite

functions.doc:
```block lang-kotlin
.cite key:{String} -> Node
```

Creates a citation to one or more bibliography entries.

The result is a label that matches with that of the bibliography entries with the given [key](cite.html). Multiple keys can be specified as a comma-separated list, producing a single combined label (e.g. `[1], [3]` or `(Einstein, 1905; Hawking, 1988)`).

Example:

`bibliography.bib`  

```block lang-bibtex
@article{einstein,
  ...
}

...
```

Quarkdown:  

```block lang-markdown
Einstein's work .cite {einstein} is fundamental to modern physics.

These results .cite {einstein, latexcompanion} are well-known.

.bibliography {bibliography.bib}
```

Result:  

```block lang-text
Einstein's work [1] is fundamental to modern physics.

These results [1], [2] are well-known.
```

#### Return

a wrapped BibliographyCitation node

#### Parameters

* **key**

  the key (or comma-separated keys) of the bibliography entries to cite

#### Throws

* [IllegalArgumentException](https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin/-illegal-argument-exception/index.html)

  if no non-blank citation key is provided

params.name: linenumbers
params.desc: whether to show line numbers

params.name: focus
params.desc: range of lines to focus on (1-based). No lines are focused if unset. Supports open ranges. Note: HTML rendering requires [linenumbers](code.html) to be enabled.

params.name: callouts
params.desc: optional dictionary of callout content, associated to their 1-based line number. Note: HTML rendering requires [linenumbers](code.html) to be enabled.

params.name: ref

params.name: code
params.desc: code content

functions.doc:
```block lang-kotlin
.code   lang:{String? = null} \
     caption:{InlineMarkdownContent? = null} \
 linenumbers:{Boolean = true} \
       focus:{Range? = null} \
    callouts:{Map<String, Any> = emptyMap()} \
         ref:{String? = null} \
        code:{EvaluableString}
-> Node
```

Creates a code block. Contrary to its standard Markdown implementation with backtick/tilde fences, this function accepts function calls within its [code](code.html) argument, hence it can be used - for example - in combination with read to load code from file.

Example of a code block loaded from file via read:  

```block lang-markdown
.code lang:{kotlin} focus:{2..5}
    .read {snippet.kt}
```

[callouts](code.html) can be specified to annotate specific lines of code with additional information:  

```block lang-markdown
.code lang:{javascript} callouts:{
    - 1: Declares the function.
    - 3: Builds the greeting.
}
    function greet() {
        const name = "World";
        return `Hello, ${name}!`;
    }
```

As a Code primitive, this function can be used in `.extend` to affect every code block in the document, including those introduced by the standard triple-backtick and triple-tilde fences:  

```block lang-markdown
.extend {code} where:{lang: .lang::equals {javascript}}
    .super linenumbers:{no}
```

#### Parameters

* **lang**

  optional language of the code
* **caption**

  optional caption
* **linenumbers**

  whether to show line numbers
* **focus**

  range of lines to focus on (1-based). No lines are focused if unset. Supports open ranges. Note: HTML rendering requires [linenumbers](code.html) to be enabled.
* **callouts**

  optional dictionary of callout content, associated to their 1-based line number. Note: HTML rendering requires [linenumbers](code.html) to be enabled.
* **ref**

  optional identifier for cross-referencing this code block elsewhere via reference
* **code**

  code content

functions.name: extend

params.name: name
params.desc: name of the existing function to extend

params.name: where
params.desc: optional condition to meet. Takes the same parameters as [body](extend.html). If the condition is not met, the call falls back to the original function definition

params.name: body
params.desc: wrapper content. Its explicit parameters, if any, must match the original function's parameter names. `.super` is implicitly available within the body

functions.doc:
```block lang-kotlin
.extend name:{String} \
       where:{Lambda? = null} \
        body:{Lambda}
-> Void
```

Defines a custom function that extends an existing one by name, wrapping its output.

Within the body, the original function is exposed as `.super`: calling it invokes the original with the arguments the wrapper was called with. The body's explicit parameters, if any, must match the original function's parameters by name and let the wrapper read those same arguments. All wrapper parameters are optional, regardless of whether the original parameters are.  

```block lang-kotlin
.function {greet}
    name:
    Hello, .name

.extend {greet}
    .super::uppercase

.greet {World}
```

> Output: `HELLO, WORLD`

The wrapper can reference the original parameters by name to alter the behavior conditionally:  

```block lang-kotlin
.extend {greet}
    name:
    .if {.name::equals {World}}
        .super::uppercase
    .ifnot {.name::equals {World}}
        .super
```

Because `.super` is the original function itself, it accepts the same arguments. Anything you pass overrides the corresponding argument the wrapper was called with, while anything you leave out falls through unchanged:  

```block lang-kotlin
.extend {greet}
    name:
    .super name:{.name::uppercase}

.greet {John}
```

> Output: `Hello, JOHN`

If [where](extend.html) is defined, it is checked against every function call. If the condition is not met, the call falls back to the original function definition. The following snippets have identical behavior:

*

  ```block lang-kotlin
    .extend {greet} where:{name: .name::equals {World}}
        name:
        .super::uppercase
  ```

*

  ```block lang-kotlin
    .extend {greet}
        name:
        .if {.name::equals {World}}
            .super::uppercase
        .ifnot {.name::equals {World}}
            .super
  ```

Function extension is the backbone of element styling, when extending primitive functions such as heading.

#### Parameters

* **name**

  name of the existing function to extend
* **where**

  optional condition to meet. Takes the same parameters as [body](extend.html). If the condition is not met, the call falls back to the original function definition
* **body**

  wrapper content. Its explicit parameters, if any, must match the original function's parameter names. `.super` is implicitly available within the body

#### Throws

* [IllegalArgumentException](https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin/-illegal-argument-exception/index.html)

  if no function named [name](extend.html) exists, or if any explicit parameter does not match an original parameter

Updates the global font configuration of the document.

Font families can be loaded from any of the following sources:

* From file (e.g. `path/to/font.ttf`)

* From URL (e.g. `https://example.com/font.ttf`)

* From system fonts (e.g. `Arial`, `Times New Roman`)

* From Google Fonts (e.g. `GoogleFonts:Roboto`).

Local and remote font resources are processed by the [media storage](https://quarkdown.com/wiki/media-storage). This means, for instance, HTML output will carry local fonts into the output directory for increased portability.

This function can be called multiple times to add multiple font configurations. Latter configurations have higher priority. This can be useful to specify fallback fonts for different glyphs. The following example applies the `Inter` font for Latin characters, and the `Ma Shan Zheng` font for Chinese characters. This happens because `Inter` does not support Chinese glyphs, so the renderer falls back to the next configuration.  

```block lang-kotlin
.font {GoogleFonts:Ma Shan Zheng}
.font {GoogleFonts:Inter}
```

The [size](font.html) parameter does not stack instead, and only the last specified size is used among all configurations.

#### Parameters

* **main**

  main font family of regular content: paragraphs, lists, blockquotes, tables and other textual elements
* **heading**

  font family of headings. If unset, [main](font.html) is applied to headings too only if the layout [theme](theme.html) does not enforce a specific heading font

functions.doc:
```block lang-kotlin
.foreach iterable:{Iterable<Any>} body:{Lambda} -> Iterable<Any>
```

Repeats content for each element of an iterable collection. The current element can be accessed via the lambda argument, which may be either explicit or implicit.  

```block lang-kotlin
.var {collection}
  - A
  - B
  - C

.foreach {.collection}
    element:
    The current element is **.element**
```

In implicit form:  

```block lang-kotlin
.foreach {.collection}
    The current element is **.1**
```

In case the iterable is destructurable (e.g. a dictionary or pair) and the lambda body has more than 1 explicit parameter, the value is destructured into components.  

```block lang-kotlin
.var {x}
    .dictionary
        - a: 1
        - b: 2
        - c: 3

.foreach {.x}
    key value:
    **.key** has value **.value**
```

The output is a collection containing the output of each iteration (mapping), so, if used as a value, this function has a meaning similar to `map` in many languages.  

```block lang-kotlin
.var {collection}
  - A
  - B
  - C

.var {mappedcollection}
    .foreach {.collection}
        item:
        .item::lowercase

.mappedcollection::first
```

> Output: `a`

Its content can also be inlined. The previous snippet can be simplified as follows:  

```block lang-kotlin
.foreach {.collection} {item: .item::lowercase}::first
```

a collection that contains the output of each iteration

#### Parameters

* **iterable**

  collection to iterate
* **body**

params.desc: content of the function. Function parameters must be **explicit** lambda parameters

functions.doc:
```block lang-kotlin
.function name:{String} body:{Lambda} -> Void
```

Defines a custom function that can be called later in the document.

The function is saved in the current context, and can be shared via mechanisms such as include or subdocuments.  

```block lang-kotlin
.function {myfunction}
    You have called this function!
```

The function can be called normally:  

```block lang-kotlin
.myfunction
```

The amount of parameters is determined by the amount of **explicit** lambda parameters.  

```block lang-kotlin
.function {add}
    a b:
    This function has two parameters, `a` and `b`.
```

Arguments can be accessed as in a function call by name:  

```block lang-kotlin
.function {greet}
    from to:
    **Hello .to** from .from
```

When calling the function, argoments can be positional, named, or a mix of both:  

```block lang-kotlin
.greet {John} {world}
```

```block lang-kotlin
.greet from:{John} to:{world}
```

A parameter might also be optional. In this case, if the corresponding argument is not provided, it will be `none`:  

```block lang-kotlin
.function {greet}
   from to?:
   **Hello .to** from .from
```

As with any none value, operations defined in the `Optionality` stdlib module help dealing with it, including simulating default values:  

```block lang-kotlin
.function {greet}
   from to?:
   **Hello .to::otherwise {world}** from .from
```

#### Parameters

* **name**

  name of the function
* **body**

  content of the function. Function parameters must be **explicit** lambda parameters

#### Throws

* [IllegalStateException](https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin/-illegal-state-exception/index.html)

functions.name: include

params.name: path
params.desc: either a path (relative or absolute with extension) to the file to include, or the name of a loadable library

params.name: sandbox
params.desc: relationship between the main context and the included file's context Values * [`share`](../com.quarkdown.stdlib/-context-sandbox/-s-h-a-r-e/index.html) * [`scope`](../com.quarkdown.stdlib/-context-sandbox/-s-c-o-p-e/index.html) * [`subdocument`](../com.quarkdown.stdlib/-context-sandbox/-s-u-b-d-o-c-u-m-e-n-t/index.html)

functions.doc:
```block lang-kotlin
.include path:{String} sandbox:{ContextSandbox = ContextSandbox.SHARE} -> Any
```

This function has two behaviors:

* Reads a Quarkdown file and includes its parsed content in the current document, using the specified [sandbox](include.html) strategy to determine what information is shared between the main context and the included file's context.

* Loads a library into the current context and includes its parsed content in the current document. Loadable libraries are fetched from the library folder (`--libs` CLI option). [sandbox](include.html) is ignored in this case.

The context of the included file is always inherited from the main file, with an updated working directory that matches the included file's location. [sandbox](include.html) defines, instead, what information is shared back to the main file's context, and how. The following modes are listed in ascending order of isolation:

* `share` (default): exchanges information bi-directionally. Changes made in the included file's context are reflected in the main file's context, and vice versa, allowing for full sharing of variables, functions and other declarations. This is represented by SharedContext.

* `scope`: like `share`, but the included file's context does not share new declarations (functions and variables) back to the main file's context. This is the behavior used within lambda blocks, such as forEach, and is represented by ScopeContext.

* `subdocument`: no information is shared back to the main file's context, only inherited from it. This also applies to the document info (metadata, title, etc.), This is the behavior used for subdocuments, and is represented by SubdocumentContext.

#### Return

the content of the file as a node if a file is included, or nothing if a library is loaded

#### Parameters

* **path**

  either a path (relative or absolute with extension) to the file to include, or the name of a loadable library
* **sandbox**

  relationship between the main context and the included file's context

  Values
  * [`share`](../com.quarkdown.stdlib/-context-sandbox/-s-h-a-r-e/index.html)
  * [`scope`](../com.quarkdown.stdlib/-context-sandbox/-s-c-o-p-e/index.html)
  * [`subdocument`](../com.quarkdown.stdlib/-context-sandbox/-s-u-b-d-o-c-u-m-e-n-t/index.html)

#### Throws

* [IllegalArgumentException](https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin/-illegal-argument-exception/index.html)

  if the loaded Quarkdown source cannot be evaluated

Displays a keyboard shortcut or key combination. Keys are displayed with platform-appropriate symbols: on macOS, modifier keys use their native symbols (e.g. `⌘` for Command, `⌥` for Option).

Any other key name is displayed as-is, capitalized.

Defines and registers a new localization table, whose entries are key-value pairs for each locale and defined by a Markdown dictionary.  

```block lang-kotlin
.localization {mytable}
    - English
        - morning: Good morning
        - evening: Good evening
    - Italian
        - morning: Buongiorno
        - evening: Buonasera
```

The localization entries can then be accessed via the [localize](localize.html) function, after setting the document language via docLanguage:  

```block lang-kotlin
.doclang {English}

```

Example, extending stdlib's localization table:  

```block lang-kotlin
.doclang {fr-CA}

.localization {std} merge:{true}
   - fr-CA
       - warning: Avertissement

.box type:{warning}
    Box content
```

In this example, the warning box will automatically feature the "Avertissement" title, since the `std:warning` localization key is accessed by the `.box` function.

#### Parameters

* **name**

  name of the localization table. Must be unique if [merge](localization.html) is false.

Finds every substring of [content](match.html) that matches the regular expression [pattern](match.html) and replaces each match with the inline content produced by [replacement](match.html).


Sets the global numbering format across the document. Numbering is applied to elements that support it, such as headings and figures.

* If a format is `none`, that kind of numbering is disabled.

* Otherwise, it accepts a string where each character represents a symbol. Some characters are reserved for counting: - `1` for decimal (`1, 2, 3, ...`) - `a` for lowercase latin alphabet (`a, b, c, ...`) - `A` for uppercase latin alphabet (`A, B, C, ...`) - `i` for lowercase roman numerals (`i, ii, iii, ...`) - `I` for uppercase roman numerals (`I, II, III, ...`)

  Any other character is considered a fixed symbol.

Sample numbering strings are `1.1.1`, `1.A.a`, `A.A`.  

```block lang-yaml
.numbering
    - headings: 1.1
    - figures: 1.a
```

If this function is *not* called, the default numbering format is picked depending on the document type.

  * `figures`, used for captioned images;

params.desc: the granularity for determining the root of the file system Values * `project` * `subdocument`

functions.doc:
```block lang-kotlin
.pathtoroot granularity:{RootGranularity = RootGranularity.PROJECT} -> String
```

Retrieves the relative path to the root of the file system. The root of the file system is determined by the working directory of either the project or the current subdocument, depending on the specified [granularity](pathtoroot.html).

If set to RootGranularity.PROJECT, the root is the parent directory of the target file being processed by the `quarkdown compile` command. If set to RootGranularity.SUBDOCUMENT, the root is the parent directory of the current subdocument file.

For example, consider the following file tree:  

```block lang-kotlin
My-Project/
├─ main.qd
├─ file.txt
├─ subdocuments/
   ├─ subdocument.qd
   ├─ file.txt
├─ utils/
   ├─ example.qd
```

If `main.qd` invokes `.pathtoroot`, the result is `.` regardless of the granularity, since the working directory is the root of the project.

Consider the content of `example.qd`:  

```block lang-kotlin
.read {.pathtoroot/file.txt}

.read {.pathtoroot granularity:{subdocument}/file.txt}
```

Now, assume `main.qd` invokes `.include {utils/example.qd}`. Regardless of the granularity, the `.pathtoroot` calls in `example.qd` return `..`, so that `My-Project/file.txt` is correctly accessed by `My-Project/utils/example.qd` through the relative path `../file.txt`.

Assume now that `subdocument.qd` is a subdocument and invokes `.include {../utils/example.qd}`.

* With RootGranularity.PROJECT, the `.pathtoroot` calls in `example.qd` return `..`, so that `My-Project/file.txt` is accessed by `My-Project/utils/example.qd` through the relative path `../file.txt`.

* With RootGranularity.SUBDOCUMENT, the `.pathtoroot` calls in `example.qd` return `../subdocuments`, so that `My-Project/subdocuments/file.txt` is accessed by `My-Project/utils/example.qd` through the relative path `../subdocuments/file.txt`.

#### Return

a string value of the relative path to the root of the file system

#### Parameters

* **granularity**

  the granularity for determining the root of the file system

  Values
  * `project`
  * `subdocument`

#### Throws

* [IllegalStateException](https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin/-illegal-state-exception/index.html)

  if the relative path cannot be determined

```block lang-kotlin
    | Lisa | 32  | LA   |
    | Mike | 19  | CHI  |
```

```block lang-kotlin
|------|-----|------|

| Lisa | 32  | LA   |
```

```block lang-kotlin
          bars:{Boolean = false} \
             x:{String? = null} \
        xrange:{Range? = null} \
         xtags:{Iterable<Any>? = null} \
             y:{String? = null} \
        yrange:{Range? = null} \
       caption:{InlineMarkdownContent? = null} \
           ref:{String? = null} \
        values:{Iterable<Any>}
-> Node
```

Creates a chart diagram on the XY plane.

The following example plots 4 points at (1, 5), (2, 2), (3, 4), (4, 10), connected by a line:  

```block lang-kotlin
.xychart
  - 5
  - 2
  - 4
  - 10
```

Multiple lines can be plotted by supplying a list of lists of points. Each list will be plotted as a separate line:  

```block lang-kotlin
.xychart
  - - 5
    - 8
    - 3
  - - 3
    - 5
    - 10
  - - 8
    - 3
    - 5
```

Complex plottings can be achieved by manipulating collections, for instance via forEach or repeat:  

```block lang-kotlin
.xychart
    .repeat {100}
        n:
        .n::pow {2}::divide {100}
```

#### Return

the generated diagram node

* **lines**

  whether to draw lines
* **bars**

  whether to draw bars
* **x**

  optional label for the X axis
* **xrange**

  optional range for the X axis. If open-ended, the range will be set to the minimum and maximum values of the X values. Incompatible with [xtags](xychart.html).
* **xtags**

  optional categorical tags for the X axis. Incompatible with [xrange](xychart.html).
* **y**

  optional label for the Y axis
* **yrange**

  optional range for the Y axis. If open-ended, the range will be set to the minimum and maximum values of the Y values
* **caption**

  optional caption. If a caption is present, the diagram will be numbered as a figure
* **ref**

  optional ID for cross-referencing via reference
* **values**

  the Y values to plot. They can be a list of points, which will be plotted as a single line, or a list of lists of points, which will be plotted as multiple lines.

#### Throws

  if both [xrange](xychart.html) and [xtags](xychart.html) are set
